stimulus: Paleomagnetists treat a rock as a tape recorder, and the first oddity is that the tape is always partly erased. Magnetite grains lock in the field at cooling, but then viscous drift creeps in, lightning strikes overwrite patches, and burial heat rewrites the rest. So the question is never "is there memory?" but "which memory is this, and how old?" Stepwise thermal demagnetization peels layers like an onion: heat to 200°C, measure, heat to 300°C, measure again, and watch the vector walk toward the origin on a Zijderveld plot. A straight line heading home means a single clean imprint. A kink means two eras are stacked. I love that kink. It feels like a palimpsest. Then there's the return-point memory in hysteresis loops, where a ferromagnet seems to "remember" the extremes of its history, the way a wiped-down whiteboard keeps ghost lines. Preisach models treat it as a crowd of tiny two-state switches, each flipping at its own threshold. That sounds oddly like voting. And the FORC diagrams, those first-order reversal curves, map the crowd's distribution. Meanwhile spin glasses do aging: wait longer, and the response slows. Does the system remember how long it sat? Fold tests and conglomerate tests ask whether the signal predates the tilting of the beds. Pebbles pointing in random directions mean the magnetism came after. Memory dated by geometry, which is strange and nice.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Stepwise 'demagnetization' of AP-1 chromatin memory
ideas.description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, EGF, or TPA), progressively erase candidate memory carriers in graded steps: titrate dominant-negative FOS (A-FOS), degron-mediated depletion of FOS/JUN, then inhibitors of chromatin remodelers (BAF) or histone writers. Measure ATAC-seq accessibility and re-stimulation response after each step. A single straight-line decay to baseline implies one mechanism, while a kink implies stacked layers, for example a fast AP-1 protein-dependent component and a slow chromatin-based one.

ideas.title: Dating the imprint: acute vs. persistent AP-1 occupancy time course
ideas.description: Run CUT&RUN/ChIP for FOS/JUN family members, ATAC-seq, and H3K27ac at multiple times after stimulus withdrawal (hours to weeks). This separates sites where AP-1 itself persists, sites where accessibility persists after AP-1 is gone, and sites that fully revert. These sites correspond to 'viscous drift' versus a locked-in imprint, and the result dates each memory by its decay.

ideas.title: FORC-style reversal-history mapping of response thresholds
ideas.description: Subject cells to defined sequences of stimulus dose up and down (minor loops with varied reversal points), and read out single-cell AP-1 reporter activity and target gene transcription. Fit a Preisach-like model of independent bistable units, with each locus or cell having its own switching threshold, to test for hysteresis and return-point memory. Compare the distribution of thresholds with and without AP-1 perturbation to show whether AP-1 sets the hysteresis.

ideas.title: Aging and dwell-time dependence test
ideas.description: Vary the time between the priming stimulus and the challenge, and also the duration of priming, in fibroblasts, keratinocytes, or macrophages. Measure whether the secondary response magnitude or kinetics depends on the interval (aging, as in spin glasses) and whether it scales with priming dose and duration. Pair this with live imaging of an AP-1 reporter and single-cell lineage tracking to see whether memory is inherited through division.

ideas.title: Overwrite and conglomerate-style controls for causality
ideas.description: Use optogenetic or inducible AP-1 pulses delivered before versus after a separate chromatin-altering event (e.g., differentiation signal or inflammatory challenge) to test whether the AP-1-dependent accessibility predates or follows it. Also compare AP-1 motif sites across cell clones given independent priming histories: shared sites suggest a deterministic imprint, whereas randomly oriented, clone-specific sites suggest the signal arose later. Complement with motif mutagenesis by CRISPR at selected enhancers to test necessity for the remembered response.
